title: Metformin: Kidneys, Contrast, and Lactic Acidosis Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Metformin improves insulin sensitivity and lowers hepatic glucose production with little hypoglycemia risk when used alone, but renal impairment, severe hypoxia/shock, major dehydration, and selected iodinated-contrast situations increase concern for metformin-associated lactic acidosis. Renal function and acute illness matter more than memorizing one automatic hold rule.
recognize: GI upset is common early in therapy and is different from the systemic deterioration of lactic acidosis.
Lactic-acidosis warning symptoms can include severe weakness, malaise, respiratory distress, abdominal symptoms, hypothermia, or altered mental status in a high-risk clinical setting.
Metformin alone usually does not cause hypoglycemia.
priorities: Verify renal function and acute clinical stability before administration when concerns are present.
Follow the current order/protocol around iodinated contrast rather than automatically withholding metformin for every imaging study.
Hold and escalate when severe hypoxia, shock, significant renal deterioration, or another major lactic-acidosis risk state develops.
assessMonitor: Trend eGFR/creatinine, hydration, glucose response, GI tolerance, and vitamin B12 status when long-term use or symptoms warrant it.
interventions: Administer with meals when prescribed to reduce GI intolerance.
Reassess renal function after contrast when the protocol requires it before restarting.
medicationSafety: Metformin is contraindicated in severe renal impairment according to product labeling.
Selected patients require temporary interruption for iodinated contrast or procedures with restricted food/fluid intake.
teaching: Tell the care team about metformin before contrast studies or procedures and report severe dehydration, breathing difficulty, or major acute illness.
delegationScope: Routine glucose measurement may be delegated where allowed; deciding whether acute illness changes medication safety requires licensed-nurse/provider review.
examTrap: Holding metformin for every contrast study without considering the actual renal function, contrast route, and current protocol—or giving it through shock and acute kidney injury because the glucose is elevated.
oneLinePearl: Metformin safety follows kidneys and perfusion, not glucose alone.

title: Sulfonylureas: Long-Lasting Hypoglycemia Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Sulfonylureas stimulate pancreatic insulin release and can cause severe or prolonged hypoglycemia, especially with missed meals, older age, renal/hepatic impairment, alcohol use, or combination glucose-lowering therapy. Food intake and hypoglycemia risk must be checked before routine administration.
recognize: Sweating, tremor, hunger, confusion, weakness, seizure, or loss of consciousness may reflect hypoglycemia.
Beta blockers can blunt adrenergic warning symptoms.
Hypoglycemia may recur after initial treatment because some sulfonylureas have prolonged effects.
priorities: Check glucose and confirm the patient can eat according to the medication plan.
Treat hypoglycemia promptly and continue monitoring for recurrence.
Report repeated lows, poor intake, renal decline, or medication mismatch.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose patterns, meal intake, renal/hepatic function, weight, and recurrent episodes.
interventions: Coordinate medication timing with meals according to the prescribed product.
Use fall and driving-safety precautions when hypoglycemia is recurrent or unrecognized.
medicationSafety: Renal or hepatic impairment may prolong hypoglycemia.
Alcohol and other glucose-lowering therapies can increase hypoglycemia risk.
redFlags: Severe hypoglycemia in an older adult living alone
teaching: Do not skip meals after taking the medication; carry a rapid glucose source and know when recurrent lows require urgent evaluation.
delegationScope: Glucose checks may be delegated where policy permits, but symptomatic hypoglycemia and medication decisions require licensed-nurse evaluation.
examTrap: Giving a sulfonylurea to a patient who is NPO simply because the scheduled medication appears on the MAR.
oneLinePearl: Sulfonylureas squeeze out insulin—missed food can turn that into a prolonged low.

title: Levothyroxine: Consistency and Absorption Matter
bottomLine: Levothyroxine replaces thyroid hormone and works best when taken consistently under the same fasting conditions. Calcium, iron, and several other products can reduce absorption; over-replacement can produce tachycardia, tremor, heat intolerance, or angina, especially in older adults with cardiac disease.
recognize: Clinical improvement is gradual; changing doses day-to-day based on symptoms is unsafe.
Persistent fatigue may reflect under-replacement but is nonspecific.
Palpitations, tremor, insomnia, or unexplained weight loss may suggest excessive thyroid-hormone effect.
priorities: Administer consistently on an empty stomach according to product instructions.
Separate interacting calcium/iron products by the prescribed interval.
Report new chest pain, marked tachycardia, or significant symptoms after dose changes.
assessMonitor: Trend TSH/free T4 as ordered, heart rate, weight, symptoms, adherence, and interacting medications/supplements.
interventions: Keep the timing and formulation as consistent as possible and communicate major product changes to the prescriber/pharmacist.
medicationSafety: Levothyroxine is not a weight-loss drug; excessive dosing can cause serious cardiovascular toxicity.
Absorption may be reduced by calcium, iron, certain antacids, bile-acid sequestrants, and some foods/medications.
redFlags: Marked agitation or hyperthermia after excessive exposure
teaching: Take levothyroxine the same way every day and tell the clinician about calcium, iron, antacids, supplements, pregnancy, or major weight changes.
delegationScope: Medication administration may be within LPN/LVN scope; interpretation of thyroid labs and dose adjustment remains prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Giving levothyroxine together with a calcium supplement because both are scheduled in the morning.
oneLinePearl: Levothyroxine works on consistency: empty stomach, separated interactions, no self-adjusting.

title: Methimazole: Fever or Sore Throat Means Check the Blood Count
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Methimazole reduces thyroid-hormone synthesis. The high-yield safety threats are agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity: fever or sore throat requires prompt evaluation, and jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, or right-upper-quadrant symptoms require liver assessment.
recognize: Rash and GI upset can occur, but fever/sore throat cannot be dismissed as a routine viral illness during therapy.
Over-treatment can produce hypothyroidism.
Pregnancy changes antithyroid-drug selection and requires specialist management.
priorities: Report fever, sore throat, or other infection symptoms promptly and follow orders for CBC/differential evaluation.
Assess jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, or abdominal symptoms for possible liver injury.
Monitor thyroid-function tests as ordered.
assessMonitor: Trend thyroid symptoms, TSH/free T4, CBC when clinically indicated, liver tests when symptoms suggest injury, and pregnancy status.
interventions: Reinforce consistent dosing and follow-up rather than stopping/restarting based on symptoms alone.
medicationSafety: Agranulocytosis can be life-threatening.
Methimazole has important fetal risks during pregnancy, especially early pregnancy; therapy is clinician-directed rather than independently stopped.
redFlags: Hemoptysis or renal symptoms suggesting vasculitis
teaching: Seek prompt medical advice for fever or sore throat and tell the prescriber immediately about pregnancy or plans for pregnancy.
delegationScope: Medication administration may be delegated only within policy; infection and hepatic-toxicity assessment require licensed-nurse/provider review.
examTrap: Telling a patient taking methimazole to use OTC cold medicine and wait several days for fever and sore throat to improve.
oneLinePearl: Methimazole + fever/sore throat = think agranulocytosis until evaluated.

title: Benzodiazepines: Sedation, Dependence, and Withdrawal
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Benzodiazepines enhance inhibitory CNS activity and can cause sedation, falls, respiratory depression, misuse, physical dependence, and dangerous withdrawal. The combination with opioids, alcohol, or other CNS depressants substantially increases respiratory risk, and chronic therapy should not be stopped abruptly.
recognize: Drowsiness, slowed reaction time, ataxia, and confusion are common safety concerns.
Older adults are particularly vulnerable to falls and delirium.
Abrupt withdrawal after physical dependence can cause severe anxiety, agitation, delirium, or seizures.
priorities: Assess sedation, respiratory rate, oxygenation when indicated, falls, and concurrent opioids/alcohol/CNS depressants.
Use fall precautions and avoid unnecessary dose stacking.
Escalate marked oversedation, hypoventilation, or withdrawal seizure.
assessMonitor: Trend level of consciousness, respiratory status, gait, cognition, duration/frequency of use, and withdrawal symptoms during tapering.
interventions: Use a clinician-directed gradual taper for discontinuation after dependence develops.
Support non-drug anxiety/sleep strategies when appropriate.
medicationSafety: FDA boxed warnings address abuse, misuse, addiction, physical dependence, and withdrawal.
Opioid co-use can cause profound sedation and respiratory depression.
teaching: Avoid alcohol, do not combine with opioids unless specifically managed, and never stop chronic use suddenly without a taper plan.
delegationScope: Sedation and respiratory assessment require licensed-nurse judgment; medication administration follows state/facility scope.
examTrap: Stopping a long-term benzodiazepine abruptly because the patient appears overly sleepy.
oneLinePearl: Benzos depress and depend: watch breathing, falls, combinations, and withdrawal.
sourceBasis: FDA Benzodiazepine Drug Class Boxed Warning and Drug Safety Communication

title: SSRIs: Suicidality, Serotonin Syndrome, and Discontinuation
bottomLine: SSRIs are commonly used for depression and anxiety disorders, but nursing safety includes monitoring for emergent suicidal thinking after initiation/dose changes, serotonin syndrome with interacting drugs, bleeding risk, hyponatremia in susceptible patients, and discontinuation symptoms if stopped abruptly.
recognize: Therapeutic benefit usually develops over time rather than after the first dose.
Agitation, tremor, hyperreflexia/clonus, fever, diarrhea, and autonomic instability suggest serotonin toxicity.
Older adults and patients taking diuretics may be more vulnerable to hyponatremia.
priorities: Assess suicide risk directly when mood worsens or behavior changes.
Review serotonergic interactions such as MAOIs, linezolid, tramadol, lithium, and St. John's wort.
Escalate serotonin-syndrome findings or severe hyponatremic neurologic symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend mood, suicidal thinking, sleep, activation, sodium when clinically indicated, bruising/bleeding, GI effects, and adherence.
interventions: Use clinician-directed gradual discontinuation when possible to reduce withdrawal symptoms.
Encourage consistent daily dosing and follow-up.
medicationSafety: SSRIs/SNRIs carry warnings about suicidal thoughts/behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients.
MAOI combinations are contraindicated because of serotonin-syndrome risk.
teaching: Do not expect immediate mood improvement or stop abruptly; report suicidal thoughts, severe agitation, fever/tremor, or unusual bleeding.
delegationScope: Suicide-risk, neurologic, and adverse-effect assessment require licensed-nurse judgment.
examTrap: Assuming worsening suicidal thinking cannot be medication-related because the antidepressant was started to reduce suicide risk.
oneLinePearl: SSRIs need time—but safety monitoring starts immediately.

title: Atypical Antipsychotics: Movement, Metabolic, and NMS Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Atypical antipsychotics can improve psychosis and mood symptoms but require monitoring for extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, metabolic changes, orthostasis, QT risk, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. New fever plus severe rigidity and autonomic instability is an emergency.
recognize: Acute dystonia, akathisia, and parkinsonism can occur after dopamine blockade.
Tardive dyskinesia causes repetitive involuntary movements and may persist.
Weight gain, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia vary by agent.
priorities: Assess abnormal movements, rigidity, fever, mental status, orthostasis, weight/metabolic trends, and fall risk.
Hold/escalate suspected NMS according to emergency protocol.
Report new involuntary movements early rather than waiting for them to become severe.
assessMonitor: Trend weight/BMI, glucose, lipids, BP, movement-disorder screening, sedation, prolactin-related symptoms, and ECG risk when indicated.
interventions: Use fall precautions with sedation or orthostasis and support nutrition/activity counseling without stigmatizing language.
medicationSafety: Older adults with dementia-related psychosis have an increased mortality warning with antipsychotic use; risperidone is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.
NMS requires immediate medication discontinuation and emergency management.
teaching: Report fever/rigidity, uncontrollable movements, severe restlessness, fainting, or major weight/glucose changes.
delegationScope: Movement and mental-status assessment require licensed-nurse evaluation; medication administration follows state/facility scope.
examTrap: Treating severe fever and rigidity as worsening psychosis and giving another antipsychotic dose.
oneLinePearl: Antipsychotic safety spans movement, metabolism, pressure, rhythm, and NMS.

title: NSAIDs: GI Bleeding, Kidneys, Heart, and Pregnancy
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: NSAIDs reduce pain, fever, and inflammation but can cause GI ulcer/bleeding, kidney injury, fluid retention, cardiovascular risk, and important pregnancy complications. Older age, CKD, anticoagulants, steroids, prior ulcer, dehydration, and heart failure raise risk.
recognize: Melena, hematemesis, unexplained anemia, or epigastric pain may signal GI injury.
Falling urine output, edema, weight gain, or rising creatinine can reflect renal/hemodynamic effects.
Many OTC cold and pain products contain NSAIDs, creating duplicate exposure.
priorities: Review GI-bleed, renal, cardiovascular, anticoagulant, and pregnancy risk before routine use.
Report black stools, vomiting blood, acute kidney injury, or new heart-failure symptoms promptly.
Check OTC duplication.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, edema/weight, renal function when indicated, GI symptoms, hemoglobin/bleeding signs, and medication combinations.
interventions: Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary duration when prescribed.
Support gastroprotection when ordered for high-risk patients.
medicationSafety: FDA advises avoiding NSAIDs around 20 weeks or later in pregnancy unless specifically directed, with stronger avoidance later in gestation; low-dose aspirin for selected pregnancy indications is a distinct clinician-directed exception.
NSAIDs can blunt diuretic/antihypertensive effects and worsen renal perfusion in susceptible patients.
redFlags: Pregnancy with unapproved NSAID exposure and concern
teaching: Check OTC labels, avoid taking multiple NSAID products together, and ask before using them in pregnancy, CKD, anticoagulation, or prior ulcer disease.
delegationScope: Risk assessment and response to bleeding/renal deterioration require licensed-nurse evaluation.
examTrap: Recommending ibuprofen as a harmless OTC option to a patient on anticoagulation with prior GI bleeding and CKD.
oneLinePearl: NSAIDs can hurt stomach, kidneys, heart, and pregnancy—screen the patient before the pill.
sourceBasis: FDA NSAID Drug Safety Communications and Prescribing Information

title: Acetaminophen: Count Every Product
bottomLine: Acetaminophen is found in many prescription and OTC combination products, so the nursing safety task is to count the total daily exposure from every source and recognize overdose early. Excess dosing can cause severe hepatic injury even when early symptoms seem mild.
recognize: Cold/flu, sleep, headache, and opioid combination products may contain acetaminophen under different names or abbreviations.
Early overdose may cause nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, or few symptoms before liver injury becomes apparent.
Liver disease and heavy alcohol use change the safety context and require clinician-specific guidance.
priorities: Review all prescription and OTC products for duplicate acetaminophen.
Follow the ordered/label maximum and patient-specific limits rather than assuming all patients can take the same amount.
Escalate suspected overdose promptly because antidotal treatment is time-sensitive.
assessMonitor: Assess total dose history, time of ingestion, liver risk factors, symptoms, and ordered acetaminophen level/liver tests in overdose evaluation.
interventions: Contact emergency/poison-management resources according to protocol for suspected overdose and prepare for N-acetylcysteine when ordered.
medicationSafety: FDA warns that too much acetaminophen can cause liver failure and death.
Do not use multiple acetaminophen-containing products simultaneously unless the total dose has been explicitly reconciled.
redFlags: Repeated supratherapeutic dosing in a high-risk patient
teaching: Read every Drug Facts label and recognize acetaminophen/APAP in combination products; more medicine does not produce safer or better pain relief.
delegationScope: Medication-history collection may be shared, but overdose risk assessment and treatment escalation require licensed-nurse/provider management.
examTrap: Giving scheduled acetaminophen without counting the acetaminophen already present in the patient's PRN combination product.
oneLinePearl: Acetaminophen safety starts by adding every source together.

title: Proton Pump Inhibitors: Use the Indication, Watch Long-Term Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: PPIs suppress gastric acid and are effective for several acid-related disorders, but long-term therapy should retain a clear indication. Nursing safety includes correct administration, medication-interaction review, and recognition of persistent diarrhea, hypomagnesemia, kidney inflammation, B12 deficiency, and fracture risk in susceptible long-term users.
recognize: Persistent watery diarrhea during PPI therapy can reflect C. difficile-associated disease rather than simple medication GI upset.
Long-term hypomagnesemia may present with weakness, tremor, tetany, seizure, or dysrhythmia.
PPIs do not make alarm GI symptoms such as bleeding, progressive dysphagia, or unexplained weight loss safe to ignore.
priorities: Verify the indication and prescribed timing relative to meals for the specific PPI/product.
Review important interactions, including drug-specific issues such as omeprazole with clopidogrel.
Escalate GI bleeding, severe persistent diarrhea, renal deterioration, or significant electrolyte symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend symptom control, duration/indication, magnesium/B12/renal status when clinically indicated, fracture risk, and recurrent diarrhea.
interventions: Use the shortest appropriate duration when the clinical indication permits and follow clinician-directed deprescribing plans rather than abruptly stopping required therapy.
medicationSafety: FDA labeling warns about acute tubulointerstitial nephritis, C. difficile-associated diarrhea, fracture, B12 deficiency, and hypomagnesemia with PPIs.
Drug interactions vary by agent.
teaching: Take the medication as directed and tell the clinician if long-term use has no clear ongoing indication or if severe diarrhea, bleeding, or swallowing difficulty develops.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within LPN/LVN scope; assessment of alarm symptoms and long-term adverse effects requires licensed-nurse/provider review.
examTrap: Continuing an indefinite PPI automatically because it has been on the medication list for years without checking the indication or adverse effects.
oneLinePearl: PPIs work well—but long-term use still needs a reason and monitoring.
